name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is the compiled, general purpose language standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 and first released in 1985. In AI work it is the performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it buys direct control of memory and speed at the cost of manual complexity, and that the official site is a standards and community hub rather than a tutorial.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language whose standardization is stewarded by the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 committee, with isocpp.org as its official site. It first appeared in 1985, and the site notes it is now more than 45 years since the language was first conceived. Within AI it occupies the performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++. That places it below the notebook and framework layer, in the runtimes, kernels and serving engines that actually execute models.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete AI jobs C++ serves are the ones where space and time constraints are real: training and inference engines, custom CUDA kernels, data pipelines, model serving and edge deployment. The site's own framing supports this, describing sustained industry demand for programmers who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints, and highlighting standard library performance enhancers such as std::simd and std::execution in C++26. It is strongest where Python is too slow or too memory hungry, and where a runtime must be embedded in another system. The official material does not rank C++ against alternatives for any specific AI task.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: C++ has a reputation for a steep learning curve, and nothing on the official site contradicts that. Prerequisites are real: some systems knowledge such as memory layout, compilation and linking, plus enough mathematics to follow the numerical code you intend to write. The site itself is a standards and community hub, carrying blog posts, standardization mailings, meeting minutes, survey announcements and conference promotions, so a beginner will not find a structured tutorial there. What it does offer is visibility into where the language is going, including memory safety profiles and reflection, which matters for anyone committing years to it.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around C++ is large and active. The site documents an annual global C++ developer survey, with a 100 page 2025 report and a 145 page 2026 report including all write-in responses forwarded to the standards committee and to tool vendors. Working groups meet regularly, including SG14 for low latency, games, embedded and financial trading, and SG19 for machine learning, whose minutes appear repeatedly across the standardization pages. Compiler support is tracked in detail, for example GCC 16.1 shipping C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening. CppCon runs annually, with CppCon 2026 starting September 12 in Aurora, Colorado.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for production performance rather than quick experiments. The site's emphasis falls on efficiency, memory safety hardening, std::simd, std::execution and reflective metaprogramming, all of which are about speed and control rather than rapid iteration. The cost is that the same control demands more code and more care: manual memory management, longer build and debug cycles, and a smaller margin for error than a scripting language. The site does not present C++ as a prototyping language, and the common pattern it implies is prototyping elsewhere and moving the hot paths into C++.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: C++ is a current standard, not a legacy choice. The committee completed technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and voted the first additions into the working draft for C++29 in June 2026, and the site cites SlashData and IDC data documenting sustained growth in demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints. For someone choosing it for work, that means the language is actively evolving and hiring demand is documented, though the site does not quantify AI specific roles or salaries, and it does not name individual employers.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: C++ is typically used with Python rather than instead of it, in a polyglot pattern where Python handles experimentation, orchestration and glue, and C++ handles the kernels, runtimes and serving paths underneath. The site's own examples fit this: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. It also sits beside CUDA for GPU work and beside C for low level interfaces. The official material describes the language and its standardization, not a prescribed pairing with any particular framework, so the exact boundary is a design decision rather than a documented rule.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The clearest weakness the site acknowledges is memory safety. Undefined behavior is being catalogued in a new C++29 annex as a first step toward addressing it systematically, and draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety guarantees are still being prototyped and targeted at C++29, so that work is not finished. Reflection and contracts are similarly in progress. The site does not say how quickly profiles will be adopted by compilers or vendors, does not give benchmarks comparing C++ with other languages for AI workloads, and does not offer a beginner curriculum, so questions about learning paths and real world performance remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
